questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/7dc83cbf45ec3025ad33552ce889c7ecb2daf73b426bc2fd10ec932f3311c92a.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{7\pi }{6},$ shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{(4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{16+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{16+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +1+15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{17+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Since $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({sec}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta +9{sec}^{6}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi $ ?
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta })^{2}+{(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )+\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta }{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1-{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )[1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta +4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{5-3\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta })^{2}+{(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\text{ }\,\pi \end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =3(\frac{\pi }{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +{sec}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta (1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sec}^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find a definite integral with respect to $\theta$ that's equivalent to $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-\sin{\theta}\,$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq  \pi,$ shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

$$
L=	\int_C \,\textrm d s =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=1-\sin{\theta},$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = -\cos{\theta}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/a55339eae9b193813ab696538c85696ad5f4267e2e31513bdb2c8998cd711311.png)

  

Calculate $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2(1+\sin\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq {\pi},$ shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

$$
L=	\int_C \,\textrm d s =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1+\sin\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\cos{\theta}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+4{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following identities:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})=1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting our integral using the above identities, we can evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }|\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =4\sqrt{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}((0+1)-(-1+0)) \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$
